overview: Liechtenstein is a small Alpine principality with a much longer history than this map record suggests. The principality dates from 1719 and became sovereign in 1806. Its mapped interval of 1994 to 2020 is a dataset window, not the country’s lifespan. Modern Liechtenstein combines a hereditary prince, elected institutions and internationally connected industries.

periods.title: A modern principality
periods.summary: This imported record opens long after the state’s establishment.

periods.title: European economic cooperation
periods.summary: Liechtenstein joined the European Economic Area in 1995; the map stops in 2020 without a political collapse.

sections.title: A pocket-sized machine with a big job

items.text: An earlier industrial success helped shape the modern country: the Curta mechanical calculator. Curt Herzstark brought his invention to Liechtenstein after surviving imprisonment in Buchenwald. The princely family founded the Contina company in 1946, and its Mauren factory was completed in 1948.

The smaller Curta was only 53 millimetres across and 85 millimetres high, yet could display an eleven-digit answer. The larger model extended that to fifteen digits. These were precision mechanical instruments small enough to carry, decades before pocket electronic calculators became ordinary.

Curtas came in protective tins. An advertising leaflet from about 1949 or 1950 pictured the calculator beside chess pieces to explain its size. Museum exhibits preserve prototypes, photographs and brochures, allowing us to follow an invention into factory production and customers’ hands.

sections.title: What people made for other countries

items.text: After 1945, industrial production increasingly concentrated on specialised technology. Examples included Hilti fastening equipment, Hoval heating and air systems, and vacuum technology at Balzers. A small country could manufacture components and tools for projects far beyond its own borders.

Other industries served very different daily needs: precision mechanical parts, dental products, convenience food and electronic connectors. These examples help explain why modern Liechtenstein’s economy cannot be understood only through castles and banks. Workshops and factories were also central to its transformation.

In its 2018 United Nations review, Liechtenstein described vocational training and academic study as alternative routes for young people. Its dual education system connected education with preparation for skilled employment. Learning a trade was an established part of the country’s educational landscape.

A family-law change taking effect in January 2015 made joint custody the usual arrangement after separation or divorce. The same United Nations review discussed this change as a response to evolving family life and children’s rights.

An independent human-rights institution began operating in 2017. It incorporated the Ombuds Office for Children and Young People, which had existed since 2009. An ombuds office gives people a place to raise concerns about rights and treatment by institutions.

Women obtained the national vote in 1984, after proposals had failed in 1971 and 1973. The first woman entered parliament in 1986. These changes were therefore quite recent when the map’s modern record begins in 1994.

Voters approved enlarging parliament to twenty-five members in 1988. The upper and lower parts of the country elected fifteen and ten respectively. The parliament’s own history explains this arrangement as protection for the smaller Lower Country district.

Article 2 of the 1921 constitution says state authority is anchored “im Fürsten und im Volke”, meaning “in the Prince and in the people”. This is the German wording in the consolidated constitutional text. The phrase captures the combination of monarchy and popular government.

Article 6 identifies German as the state and official language. The constitution itself is consequently also an example of formal written German used in public life. Its legal vocabulary differs from the informal language that families use at home.

ending.text: Liechtenstein continued beyond the map’s 2020 endpoint. Its long-established sovereignty and European economic links did not end when this imported record stopped.
